For an alternating form, choose nonzero $v$, choose $w$ with $B(v,w)=1$, split off the nondegenerate plane they span, and induct on its orthogonal complement. Applying the same argument after quotienting by the radical shows that any rank-$r$ symmetric matrix is congruent to $\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0)$ and any rank-$r$ alternating matrix is congruent to $J_r\oplus0$, with $r$ even in the latter case.

Conversely, every Gram matrix has rank at most $\dim V$, since it factors through the linear map $k^t\to V$ whose columns are the chosen vectors. For every canonical rank-$r$ matrix in step 1.1, choose $r$ vectors in $V$ giving that standard form and set the remaining vectors to zero. If $S$ is an invertible $t\times t$ matrix satisfying $S^\mathsf{T}GS=C$ for an arbitrary rank-$r$ matrix $G$ and its canonical matrix $C$, multiplying the chosen tuple by $S^{-1}$ gives Gram matrix $G$. This realizes every matrix in the rank-bounded image.

Let $f_1,f_2:k^t\to V$ be the surjective maps defined by two tuples with the same rank-$m$ Gram matrix $G$. For $c\in k^t$, $f_i(c)=0$ implies $Gc=0$; conversely $Gc=0$ implies $B(f_i(c),f_i(d))=0$ for every $d$, and surjectivity plus nondegeneracy gives $f_i(c)=0$. Thus $\ker f_1=\ker f_2$, so $T(f_1(c))=f_2(c)$ is a well-defined linear isomorphism. The equality of Gram matrices makes $T$ preserve the form. It is the unique isometry carrying the first tuple to the second, and a form-preserving map fixing a spanning tuple is the identity.

A rank-$r$ symmetric matrix is equivalent to its kernel, a $(t-r)$-plane, and a nondegenerate symmetric form on the $r$-dimensional quotient. The finitely many standard graph charts cover the Grassmannian of $(t-r)$-planes, and each chart has $r(t-r)$ coordinates. Over such a chart, symmetric forms on the quotient have $r(r+1)/2$ free coordinates, and nondegeneracy is the nonvanishing of the determinant, an open condition. Thus this stratum has dimension $r(t-r)+r(r+1)/2=rt-r(r-1)/2$. In the alternating case the form space has dimension $r(r-1)/2$ and nondegeneracy is again open, so the stratum dimension is $r(t-r)+r(r-1)/2=rt-r(r+1)/2$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and let $\delta\in R$. A set partition of a finite set is a collection of disjoint nonempty subsets, called blocks, whose union is the whole set; a perfect matching is a set partition whose blocks each have size two. For $a,b\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$, place $a$ ordered input vertices on a top edge and $b$ ordered output vertices on a bottom edge. The Brauer module $\mathcal B_\delta(a,b)$ is the free $R$-module on perfect matchings of these $a+b$ vertices. It is zero if $a+b$ is odd. The partition module $\mathcal P_\delta(a,b)$ is the free $R$-module on set partitions of the same vertices.

For $D\in\mathcal B_\delta(a,b)$ and $E\in\mathcal B_\delta(b,c)$, glue the output vertices of $D$ to the corresponding input vertices of $E$. Take the equivalence relation generated by the two matchings and these identifications. Each equivalence class meeting an outer vertex consists of exactly two outer vertices and gives an edge of a new matching. Each class meeting no outer vertex is a closed loop. Define $E\circ D=\delta^\ell H$, where $H$ is the resulting outer matching and $\ell$ is the number of removed loops. For partition diagrams use the equivalence relation generated by the two partitions and the same gluing; each outer equivalence class gives a block and each class with no outer vertices contributes one factor $\delta$. Extend composition $R$-bilinearly.

The identity at $a$ is the matching joining input $i$ to output $i$, respectively the partition into those $a$ through-blocks. Juxtaposition defines tensor product on objects by addition and on diagrams by disjoint union. The Brauer algebra $B_a(\delta)$ and partition algebra $P_a(\delta)$ are the endomorphism algebras at object $a$.

These are abstract diagram modules over arbitrary $R$. This definition asserts no faithfulness of any tensor representation.

Glue both middle interfaces at once, and let $\sim$ be the least equivalence relation generated by all diagram edges or blocks and both sets of interface identifications. The relation $\sim$ is independent of the order in which the two interfaces are glued, since the least equivalence relation generated by a fixed set of pairs is unique. Thus both bracketings retain exactly the same equivalence classes meeting the outer boundary.

The classes meeting no outer vertex are also the same for both bracketings. Any class removed when the first two diagrams are composed meets neither of their exposed boundaries, so it contains no vertex of the third diagram; it can never merge with another class in the second composition. Conversely, every final class meeting no outer vertex is either removed at the first composition or is removed at the second. Hence the sum of the two loop counts in either bracketing equals the number of classes of $\sim$ meeting no outer vertex.

By [F1], each bracketing therefore has the same outer diagram and coefficient $\delta^\ell$, with the same integer $\ell$. The two bracketings agree on basis diagrams, so bilinearity gives associativity on the free modules. The identity diagrams add no new equivalence identifications and remove no class; they act as left and right units.

derivations.claim: For basis tuples $I,K$ on the external boundary, the matrix coefficient of $\Phi(E)\Phi(D)$ is the sum over middle tuples $J$ of $\Phi(D)_{I,J}\Phi(E)_{J,K}$. The equalities imposed by the two diagrams generate exactly the blocks of the stacked partition. Each generated block meeting an outer label has its index fixed by that label; each block wholly in the middle has $N$ independent choices. Hence the coefficient is $N^\ell$ when the outer labels satisfy the stacked partition and zero otherwise, where $\ell$ is the number of removed middle blocks. By [F1] this equals the coefficient of $\Phi(E\circ D)$, so $\Phi$ respects multiplication; [F2] supplies associativity of the domain algebra.

Index a tensor basis vector by an $r$-tuple $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^r$. A matrix coefficient of an operator is indexed by a pair $(I,J)$. The operator commutes with all basis permutations exactly when its matrix coefficient is constant on simultaneous $S_N$-orbits of $(I,J)$. Two such pairs lie in the same orbit exactly when they have the same equality pattern on the $2r$ labels: a permutation maps one pair to the other if and only if it maps their distinct used indices block by block. Thus orbit indicator matrices form a basis of the commutant over every field.

For a partition diagram $d$, the matrix coefficient of $\Phi(d)$ is $1$ exactly when labels joined by a block of $d$ receive equal indices. It is therefore the sum of orbit indicators $E_\pi$ over exact equality patterns $\pi$ coarser than $d$ and having at most $N$ blocks. The finite-poset zeta matrix is triangular with diagonal entries one, so its inverse $\mu$ gives an invertible change of basis from the diagram basis to the elements $x_d$. Möbius inversion therefore gives $\Phi(x_d)=E_d$ if $d$ is realizable and $0$ otherwise.

An exact pattern $d$ is realizable precisely when it has at most $N$ blocks, since one can assign distinct indices to its blocks. Its orbit indicator is then nonzero, and different exact patterns have disjoint supports, so these images are linearly independent. Step 2.1 shows they span the image and that every $x_d$ with more than $N$ blocks maps to zero; hence the kernel and image have the stated forms. The full diagram basis is independent in the image exactly when every partition of $2r$ labels has at most $N$ blocks, which is equivalent to $N\ge2r$. No division by $N!$ was used, so the argument is valid in every characteristic.

Interchange expands every word into such an expression. Conversely, draw the finitely many edges of a matching as polygonal paths with distinct heights for all crossings and local extrema. Slicing at intervening heights gives a regular expression for that matching. The displayed relations and their horizontal and vertical reflections hold by following their boundary pairs; only $AU$ removes a component, and it removes exactly one. Consequently evaluation gives a surjection from the presented $R$-linear category to [F1]. It remains to prove injectivity, without using any tensor representation.

We give the regular-expression reduction explicitly. The position of an elementary map is the number of identity strands to its left plus one. Elementary maps supported on disjoint intervals commute by interchange, with the positions after insertion/deletion adjusted by two. Define bending on a word $D:a\to b$ by $R(D)=(D\otimes I)(1_{a-1}\otimes U)$ and, for $b\ge1$, $L(D)=(1_{b-1}\otimes A)(D\otimes I)$. Commuting the extra cup or cap past each padded factor by interchange and then applying the snake relation gives $LR(D)\sim D$ and $RL(D)\sim D$. Here $\sim$ means equality using the proposed relations. Thus equivalence of words is preserved and reflected by bending. It is also preserved and reflected by multiplication by permutation words: to undo an adjacent crossing multiply by that crossing and use $X^2=1$; undo a permutation one crossing at a time. Bend all input vertices to outputs and permute outputs so that the target matching is the adjacent matching $U^{\otimes r}$. These are invertible operations on the diagram basis as well as on words, so it suffices to reduce every regular expression for a scalar multiple of $U^{\otimes r}$.

The local reduction used below is the following cup-train calculation. Start with a cup at position $a$ and successively cross its right leg past $s$ strands: $T_s=X_{a+s}\cdots X_{a+1}U_a$; all subscripts denote positions at the appropriate intermediate object. A cap at position $j$ outside $[a-1,a+s+1]$ commutes below this train. Within that interval it shortens the expression, except that $s=0,j=a$ removes a loop and gives $\delta$. Here are the reductions covering the interval. At $j=a+s$, use $AX=A$ to remove the last crossing. At $j=a+s+1$, use the slide relation to move the cap left across the last crossing, commute that crossing below the other disjoint factors, and repeat; after $s$ repetitions the cap is next to the cup at position $a+1$, and the snake relation deletes that cap and cup. At $a\le j<a+s$, commute the cap down to the first crossing meeting it, use the slide relation, and cancel the two resulting equal adjacent crossings with $X^2=1$ (when the crossing meets the cup use $XU=U$ instead). At $j=a-1$, commute down to the cup and apply the reflected snake relation. Each operation replaces a word with strictly fewer elementary factors, apart from the loop factor which is retained as a scalar.

A crossing outside the same interval commutes below $T_s$. For $a+1\le j<a+s$, commute it to the two consecutive crossings it meets, apply the braid relation, and commute the resulting crossing below the cup; this writes $X_jT_s$ as a train followed by one crossing. At the right endpoint $j=a+s$, cancel the repeated last crossing. At $j=a$, commute towards the cup, use the cup-slide relation and then cancel repeated crossings, or use $XU=U$ when $s=0$. At $j=a+s+1$, the expression is the train $T_{s+1}$. At $j=a-1$, the reflected cup-slide relation moves the starting cup one position left: the expression is a reflected train or shortens by crossing cancellation. Apply the same calculation after reflection whenever the moving leg travels left. Thus a cap or crossing applied to a train either shortens the word (possibly extracting $\delta$), passes below the train, or extends its moving leg by one strand. Read a regular expression $D_1\cdots D_h$ from left to right, so its leftmost factor is applied last. Since a word $0\to0$ cannot consist only of a cup followed by crossings, a cap is eventually met. For $r>0$, $h\ge r$. If $h=r$, all factors are cups; because the output matching is adjacent, their final positions are odd, and interchange orders these cups to $U^{\otimes r}$. For $|A|=|B|=s\le m$, The explicit determinant expansion in [F1] gives $p(A,B)(XX^{\mathsf T})=\sum_{|C|=s}\det X_{A,C}\det X_{B,C}$. The leading term of a determinant with increasing row and column sets pairs their first indices, then their second indices, and so on: at the first column, the lexicographically largest variable available has its smallest row index. The largest summand in Cauchy–Binet has $C=(1,\ldots,s)$, by comparing the first column belonging to exactly one of two column sets. Consequently the leading monomial of this Gram minor, with coefficient one, is $\prod_{r=1}^s x_{a_r r}x_{b_r r}$.

We record the local normality transfer used here. If $A$ is a local domain essentially of finite type over $k$, $h$ is a nonzero element of its maximal ideal, and $A/hA$ is normal, then $A$ is normal. The nonzero normal local ring $A/hA$ is a domain, so $hA$ is prime. To check the assertion with Serre's criterion, first take a prime $Q$ containing $h$. The ring and its localizations are Noetherian by [F4]. By [F5], quotienting these local domains by the nonzero prime element $h$ lowers dimension by one: apply the principal ideal theorem to its prime ideal and then the affine-domain dimension formula before localization. The depth formula [F3] for a nonzerodivisor gives $\operatorname{depth}A_Q=1+\operatorname{depth}(A/hA)_{Q/hA}\ge\min(3,\dim A_Q)$. If $\dim A_Q\le2$, its quotient is regular by the $R_1$ direction of [F2]; lift its $\dim A_Q-1$ maximal-ideal generators and adjoin $h$. The maximal ideal of $A_Q$ is generated by at most $\dim A_Q$ elements, so [F6] makes $A_Q$ regular. For a prime $q$ not containing $h$, choose $Q$ minimal over $q+(h)$ in $A$. Such a prime exists since $A$ is local and $h$ belongs to its maximal ideal. The element $h$ has nonzero image in the domain $A/q$, and $Q/q$ is minimal over that image. The principal ideal theorem and dimension formula [F5] therefore give $\dim A_Q=\dim A_q+1$ and $\dim(A_Q/qA_Q)=1$. If $\dim A_q=1$, $A_Q$ is regular by the preceding observation, and so is its localization $A_q$ by [F6]. If $\dim A_q\ge2$, the depth localization inequality [F3], applied to $A_Q$ and $qA_Q$, gives $\operatorname{depth}A_q\ge\operatorname{depth}A_Q-1\ge2$. The zero-prime localization is a field. Together with the primes containing $h$, this proves $R_1$ and $S_2$, hence normality by [F2].

For a standard product discard empty factors and write its columns in reverse order, $B_q,A_q,\ldots,B_1,A_1$. This is a tableau with weakly increasing rows, strictly increasing columns, nonincreasing column lengths, and columns of each length occurring an even number of times. Its row lengths are therefore even. Conversely such a tableau has pairs of consecutive columns of equal length, and reversing its columns and grouping these pairs recovers exactly one standard product. The exponents of its leading monomial record the entries in every row; weak increase reconstructs those rows uniquely. Distinct standard products thus have distinct leading monomials. All $(m+1)$-minors vanish under the Gram map, and [F1] now shows that the induced map $R=k[z_{ij}]/I_{m+1}\longrightarrow P$ is injective. In particular $R$ is a domain.

Describe these leading exponents as arrays $a=(a_{ri})\in\mathbb N^{mt}$. Set $c_r(u)=\sum_{i\le u}a_{ri}$, with $c_r(0)=0$. The necessary and sufficient conditions are that every $c_r(t)$ is even and $c_{r+1}(u)\le c_r(u-1)$ for $1\le r<m$ and $1\le u\le t$. Indeed the latter inequalities say exactly that the $j$th entry of row $r$ is strictly smaller than the $j$th entry of row $r+1$, whenever the latter exists: count entries at most $u$ to obtain necessity, and apply the inequality with $u$ equal to that lower entry to obtain sufficiency. They imply nonincreasing row lengths. Even row lengths make their consecutive differences even, so the resulting columns have the required paired lengths. Thus these arrays form exactly the semigroup $S$ of leading monomials of $R$. It is closed under addition. If $a\in\operatorname{gp}(S)$ and $Na\in S$ for a positive integer $N$, its entries are nonnegative, the displayed inequalities hold after division by $N$, and its row sums are even since every element of $\operatorname{gp}(S)$ has that parity. Hence $a\in S$: this is saturation in the actual group of the semigroup, rather than saturation in the larger unrestricted integer lattice.

The algebra $k[S]$ is integrally closed. Here is the lattice argument. Write $L=\operatorname{gp}(S)$ and let $C$ be the cone cut out by nonnegativity and the inequalities in step 3.1. That step proves $S=C\cap L$. Inside $k[L]$, each integral linear inequality $\ell\ge0$ defines a valuation by $v_\ell(\sum b_a x^a)=\min_{b_a\ne0}\ell(a)$; the product rule follows because the associated lowest-weight Laurent polynomials have nonzero product. Its nonnegative subring is a valuation ring intersected with $k[L]$. The Laurent polynomial ring $k[L]$ is integrally closed by [F8] and denominator clearing: if $f$ is integral over a localization $U^{-1}D$ of an integrally closed domain $D$, choose $u\in U$ clearing all coefficients of its monic equation; then $uf$ is integral over $D$, hence belongs to $D$, so $f\in U^{-1}D$. This also proves the localization assertion used below. Valuation rings are integrally closed as well: a monic equation for an element of negative valuation has its highest power of strictly smallest valuation, which is impossible. The intersection of these rings, inside their common fraction field, is precisely $k[C\cap L]$, by the monomial independence in $k[L]$. Intersections of integrally closed subrings of a field are integrally closed.

We construct a finite weight degeneration, to make the normality transfer explicit. The finitely many Gram minors generate $R$, because they include all its degree-one generators $z_{ij}$. By steps 2.1 and 3.1 their leading monomials generate $S$: every standard monomial is a product of those leading monomials. Introduce one variable for each nonempty Gram minor, mapped to its leading monomial. The kernel of this monomial map is generated by finitely many binomials. This follows from Noetherianity [F4] of the finite polynomial ring, and the kernel is spanned by binomials because monomials with the same image exponent are the only linear dependencies. For each of these finitely many binomials substitute the actual Gram minors; their largest terms cancel. Repeatedly subtract the uniquely matching standard product to cancel the largest remaining term, using [F1] and step 2.1. This process terminates: all polynomials involved have one fixed ordinary degree in the $x$'s and there are only finitely many monomials of that degree. Choose a positive integer weight on the $x$ variables realizing all the strict lexicographic comparisons in this finite list of reductions and all the minor expansions; sufficiently separated positive powers realize any finite list of lexicographic comparisons.

For this weight the minors still form a basis for leading-term subduction: if highest-weight terms in a polynomial expression in the minors cancel, its highest-weight symbolic part belongs to the toric kernel from step 4.2. Express it in the finitely many binomial generators, and replace each by its recorded reduction. Each replacement lowers the weight of the cancelling part. All weights are nonnegative integers; this induction terminates. It proves that the associated graded algebra for the weight filtration on $R\subset P$ is $k[S]$. For $F_dR=\{f\in R:\deg_w f\le d\}$, its Rees algebra $T=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}(F_dR)h^d\subset R[h]$ is generated by $h$ and the finitely many $h^{d_j}p_j$, where $d_j$ is the weight of the leading monomial of the $j$th minor. Subduction proves this last assertion by induction on weight. We have $T/hT=k[S]$, $T[h^{-1}]=R[h,h^{-1}]$, and $h$ is a nonzerodivisor. The $h$ grading makes $T$ a positively graded finite algebra with $T_0=k$, since all variable weights are positive.

Apply step 1.2 to the local ring of $T$ at its homogeneous maximal ideal $M=T_{>0}$. Its quotient by $h$ is a localization of the normal ring in step 4.1, so $T_M$ is normal. To pass from the local assertion to all of $T$, let $B$ be its normalization in its fraction field; it is finite by [F7], since step 5.1 makes $T$ a finite-type domain. For every $b\in B$, the same monic equation shows that its image belongs to the normal local ring $T_M$; hence $(B/T)_M=0$. As $B/T$ is finite, multiplying denominators for a finite generating set produces $s\notin M$ with $s(B/T)=0$. Let $J=\operatorname{Ann}_T(B/T)$. For each $c\in k^\times$, grading gives the automorphism $\gamma_c(a_d)=c^da_d$ of $T$ and its fraction field. It preserves $B$ by applying it to monic equations; therefore it preserves $J$. If $a=\sum_{d\in D}a_d\in J$ has finite homogeneous support, every $\sum_dc^da_d$ lies in $J$. The distinct functions $c\mapsto c^d$ are linearly independent on the infinite field $k$ (a nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots); choosing finitely many evaluation points with invertible evaluation matrix and solving gives $a_d\in J$ for every $d$. An element of $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ integral over $R$ is then in $R[h,h^{-1}]\cap\operatorname{Frac}(R)=R$, as comparison of Laurent coefficients shows. This proves normality for $1\le m<t$. derivations.claim:
We first give an indexed shuffle identity, including an explicit way to expand its right side. Pfaffians with arbitrary ordered lists are interpreted alternatingly, and vanish on repeated indices. If $h\ge h'$ are positive even integers, $1\le s\le h'$, $U=(u_1,\ldots,u_{h+s})$, and $C=(c_1,\ldots,c_{h'-s})$, put $\epsilon(D,U\setminus D)$ equal to the sign of the permutation listing first the positions $D$ and then their complement, both increasingly. Then [given, algebra]
$$
F(U,C)=\sum_{D\subseteq[h+s],\ |D|=h}\epsilon(D,U\setminus D)P_{U_D}P_{(U_{D^c},C)}\ \in\ (P_H:|H|\ge h+2).
$$
Here is a polynomial identity proving this membership, rather than a set-theoretic rank argument. Use exterior variables $e_1,\ldots,e_{h+s},f_1,\ldots,f_{h'-s}$, in that order, and put $\Omega=\sum_{i<j}a_{u_i u_j}e_i e_j$, $\Theta=\sum_{i,j}a_{u_i c_j}e_i f_j$, and $\Psi=\sum_{i<j}a_{c_i c_j}f_i f_j$. The displayed sum is the coefficient of $e_1\cdots e_{h+s}f_1\cdots f_{h'-s}$ in
$$
\operatorname{pr}_{h+s,h'-s}\left(\frac{\Omega^{h/2}}{(h/2)!}\frac{(\Omega+\Theta+\Psi)^{h'/2}}{(h'/2)!}\right)=\sum_{2r+q=s,\ q+2l=h'-s}\frac{\Omega^{h/2+r}\Theta^q\Psi^l}{(h/2)!r!q!l!}.
$$
Here $\operatorname{pr}_{a,b}$ means projection to exterior bidegree $(a,b)$ in the $e$ and $f$ variables. For $r\ge1$, expand the coefficient of $\Omega^{h/2+r}/(h/2+r)!$: each coefficient is a Pfaffian of size $h+2r$. For $r=0$, $q=s\ge1$; expand $\Theta^q$ as a sum of products of $\theta_j f_j$, where $\theta_j=\sum_i a_{u_i c_j}e_i$, and single out its first factor. Each coefficient of $\Omega^{h/2}\theta_j/(h/2)!$ is, with its exterior sign, $P_{(U_E,c_j)}$ for $|E|=h+1$: this follows by expanding the Pfaffian along $c_j$. Expanding the remaining exterior factors gives a completely specified finite sum of larger Pfaffians times polynomials. Thus the identity proves the asserted ideal membership. Repeated actual labels cause no difficulty because the identity is alternating in the formally labelled positions. Larger Pfaffians themselves belong to the ideal of size $h+2$ by repeated expansion along the first index.

Order nonempty Pfaffian symbols by decreasing size, then lexicographically by their index words written in decreasing order; order products by first sorting their factors in this order and then lexicographically. Suppose a sorted adjacent pair $P_A,P_B$, of sizes $h\ge h'$, fails $a_j\le b_j$ for some $j\le h'$. Choose such an $s$. Apply step 1.1 to the ordered list $U=(a_s,\ldots,a_h,b_1,\ldots,b_s)$ and the fixed list consisting of $a_1,\ldots,a_{s-1}$ in the first Pfaffian and $b_{s+1},\ldots,b_{h'}$ in the second. To justify this version with fixed positions explicitly, define $H_{i,j}(A;B;U)=\sum_{|D|=i}\epsilon(D,D^c)P_{(A,U_D)}P_{(U_{D^c},B)}$, with $|A|=h-i$, $|B|=h'-j$, $|U|=i+j$. Splitting according to the factor containing the first position $x$ gives the exact recurrence [step 1.1, algebra]
$$
H_{i,j}((A_0,x);B;U)=H_{i+1,j}(A_0;B;(x,U))-(-1)^{i+j}H_{i+1,j-1}(A_0;(x,B);U).
$$
For $i+j>h$, repeatedly applying it reduces to $i=h$, where step 1.1 applies; $j$ stays positive since $i+j>h$. This proves membership in the larger-Pfaffian ideal and gives its expansion by a finite recurrence. Take $i=h-s+1$, $j=s$, $A=(a_1,\ldots,a_{s-1})$, and $B=(b_{s+1},\ldots,b_{h'})$. The resulting relation has the form
$$
\sum_{D\subseteq[h+1],\ |D|=h-s+1}\epsilon(D,D^c)P_{(a_1,\ldots,a_{s-1},U_D)}P_{(U_{D^c},b_{s+1},\ldots,b_{h'})}\ \in\ (P_H:|H|\ge h+2).
$$
The coefficient of $P_AP_B$ is $1$ up to its displayed ordering sign. Indeed $b_i\le b_s<a_s\le a_j$ for $i\le s\le j$, so the two shuffled groups have no common label. When $h=h'$, no second occurrence arises by exchanging the two factors: every changed first factor precedes $P_A$, whereas the originally sorted $P_B$ does not. Every other nonzero first factor replaces at least one of $a_s,\ldots,a_h$ by an index below $a_s$, and therefore precedes $P_A$. Every term in the larger-Pfaffian expansion has a factor of size at least $h+2$ and also precedes $P_A$. Solving this relation rewrites the offending product into strictly earlier sorted products. Sorting all factors preserves this strict decrease: the unchanged factors occur in both multisets, and the replacement introduces a factor preceding $P_A$ while the two removed factors are both at least $P_A$. All relations preserve the ordinary degree, with $\deg P_S=|S|/2$; in any fixed degree only finitely many products exist. Rewriting therefore terminates. Its terminal products are precisely chains for $\preceq$. In the quotient, factors of size greater than $m$ vanish by Pfaffian expansion, so the surviving chains are exactly those stated. This proves spanning.

For independence put $m=2n$ and introduce independent variables $x_{ij}$, $1\le i\le t$, $1\le j\le m$. Substitute [step 2.1, algebra]
$$
a_{uv}=\sum_{j=1}^n(x_{u,2j-1}x_{v,2j}-x_{v,2j-1}x_{u,2j}).
$$
Exterior expansion gives $P_S\mapsto\sum_H\det X_{S,H}$, where $H$ runs over unions of complete consecutive column pairs and $|H|=|S|$; each coefficient is $1$. If $|S|>m$ the sum is empty. Order the $x$ variables column first and then row, giving earlier columns and smaller rows priority, and use lexicographic monomial order. For $S=(s_1<\cdots<s_h)$ with $h\le m$, the unique leading monomial of its image is $d_S=\prod_{j=1}^h x_{s_j,j}$, with coefficient $1$: at each successive column the determinant term with the smallest unused row has priority, and the first $h$ columns beat every other union of column pairs. Multiplicativity gives leading monomial $\prod_a d_{S_a}$ for a standard product. Recover this product uniquely by sorting the row indices appearing in each column of its monomial increasingly; the resulting rows, read from longest to shortest, are exactly $S_1,S_2,\ldots$. Hence distinct standard products have distinct leading monomials. Their images, and therefore their residue classes, are linearly independent. For $m=0$ all entries vanish and only the empty product survives. Together with spanning this proves the assertion, including the zero-ideal case.

derivations.claim: The Gram embedding in [F1] makes $R$ a domain. We describe its monomial degeneration explicitly. Choose positive integer weights on the finitely many variables $x_{ij}$ which realize the column-first lexicographic comparisons between all terms in all the finitely many Gram images $P_S$, $|S|\le m$. Such weights exist: list the variables in that lexicographic order, give successive variables weights $N^{tm-1},N^{tm-2},\ldots,1$, and take $N>2t+1$, larger than the total degree of each polynomial being compared. Thus $d_S$ is the unique term of largest weight in each image. Filter $R$ by these ambient polynomial weights. A standard product has unique term of largest weight equal to the corresponding product of the $d_S$; these monomials are distinct by [F1]. In a linear combination of standard products the terms of maximum weight therefore do not cancel. Consequently the associated graded ring is exactly $k[\Gamma]$, where $\Gamma$ is the additive semigroup generated by the exponent vectors of all $d_S$, for even $|S|\le m$. In particular this is a filtration of the entire ring, not merely a computation of the initial terms of its generators.

Write an exponent array as $b=(b_{ij})$, put $\lambda_j=\sum_i b_{ij}$, and put $C_j(u)=\sum_{i\le u}b_{ij}$, with $C_j(0)=0$. The semigroup $\Gamma$ consists exactly of the integer arrays satisfying [step 1.1, algebra]
$$
b_{ij}\ge0,\qquad \lambda_{2r-1}=\lambda_{2r},\qquad \lambda_j\ge\lambda_{j+1},\qquad C_{j+1}(u)\le C_j(u-1)\quad(1\le j<m,\ 1\le u\le t).
$$
Necessity follows by adding these inequalities for individual increasing even rows. For sufficiency sort the row indices in each column increasingly, with multiplicities. The cumulative inequalities say that the $a$th entry of column $j$ is strictly less than the $a$th entry of column $j+1$ whenever the latter exists: a failure at value $u$ would give $C_{j+1}(u)>C_j(u-1)$, and the converse follows by taking $a=C_{j+1}(u)$. The inequalities on column lengths make a left-justified tableau; their pairwise equalities say that every row length is even. Each row is therefore an allowed $S$. Reading these rows from top to bottom gives a standard product and expresses $b$ as a sum of exponent vectors of $d_S$. All displayed conditions are homogeneous integral linear inequalities or equalities. Thus if $b$ is in the group $L$ generated by $\Gamma$ and $qb\in\Gamma$ for a positive integer $q$, then $b\in\Gamma$. More precisely $\Gamma=L\cap\mathcal C$, where $\mathcal C$ is the rational polyhedral cone cut out by the displayed conditions.

This proves normality of $k[\Gamma]$ directly. The group algebra $k[L]$ is a Laurent polynomial ring after choosing an integral lattice basis and is integrally closed by [F8]. Each defining integral linear inequality $\ell\ge0$ gives the valuation $v_\ell(\sum c_b X^b)=\min_{c_b\ne0}\ell(b)$ on its fraction field (combine equal-weight terms first); its nonnegative valuation ring is integrally closed by [F8]. The equality $\Gamma=L\cap\mathcal C$ gives [step 2.1, algebra]
$$
k[\Gamma]=k[L]\cap\bigcap_{\ell}\{f:v_\ell(f)\ge0\}.
$$
Indeed for a Laurent polynomial nonnegative minimum under every $\ell$ means that every exponent lies in $\mathcal C$. An intersection of integrally closed subrings of one field is integrally closed, by applying a monic equation in every member of the intersection. Hence the special ring of the filtration is a normal domain.

We give the lifting argument to avoid assuming normality from distinct initial terms. Let $\mathcal B=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}F_dR\,z^d\subset R[z]$ be the Rees ring of step 1.1. It is generated by $z$ and $P_Sz^{w(d_S)}$: expand an element in the standard basis, and use the absence of highest-weight cancellation in step 1.1. It is a finitely generated domain, hence Noetherian by [F2], with $\mathcal B/(z)=k[\Gamma]$, and $\mathcal B[z^{-1}]=R[z,z^{-1}]$. Retain also the ordinary grading $\deg(P_S)=|S|/2$ and $\deg z=0$; then $\mathcal B_0=k[z]$ and all other generators have positive ordinary degree. We use the following local normality argument. For a finite-type domain $D$ over a field and a nonzero element $z$, if $(D/(z))_{\mathfrak p}$ is normal, then $D_{\mathfrak p}$ is normal for every prime $\mathfrak p$ containing $z$. To check this by [F3], localize at such $\mathfrak p$. At a prime $Q$ containing $z$, [F4] increases depth by one from the quotient and [F6] increases dimension by one, so the $S_2$ bounds follow from $S_2$ of the quotient. Height-one primes containing $z$ have field quotients, so their local rings are regular by [F6]. Height-zero primes of the domain localize to its fraction field and are regular. For $Q$ not containing $z$ and of positive height, choose a prime $P$ minimal over $Q+(z)$ in this local ring. Applied to the corresponding primes in the original affine domain, [F5] gives $\operatorname{ht}P=\operatorname{ht}Q+1$ and $\dim(D_P/QD_P)=1$. If $\operatorname{ht}Q=1$, the quotient of $D_P$ by $z$ is a normal one-dimensional local domain, hence regular by $R_1$ in [F3]; [F6] makes $D_P$ regular of dimension two and then makes its localization $D_Q$ regular. If $\operatorname{ht}Q\ge2$, the quotient has depth at least two by [F3], so $D_P$ has depth at least three by [F4]; the depth-localization inequality in [F4] $\operatorname{depth}D_Q\ge\operatorname{depth}D_P-\dim(D_P/QD_P)$ gives depth at least two at $Q$. Thus $R_1$ and $S_2$ hold throughout the local ring, which proves the assertion. All these applications concern Noetherian local rings by [F2], nonzero regular elements because the Rees ring is a domain, and primes of an affine domain, as required by [F3]–[F6]. Applied to $\mathcal B$, step 3.1 proves normality at every point of the fiber $z=0$.

For completeness, this local conclusion controls every fiber here. The normalization is finite and its nonnormal locus is closed by [F7]. The nonnormal locus of $\mathcal B$ is stable under both its ordinary grading action and its filtration grading action: each scaling is a ring automorphism, extends to the fraction field, and preserves integral elements and therefore the normalization quotient. This uses no assertion that normalization itself has a chosen grading. If it contained a point over $z=c\ne0$, its closure under the ordinary grading action would contain the point of the section with all positive-ordinary-degree generators zero and $z=c$: the orbit map extends to scaling parameter zero. The filtration grading action then gives all points of that section with $z\ne0$; closedness gives its point at $z=0$, contradicting step 4.1. By [F9], over the algebraically closed field $k$ a nonempty closed subset has a $k$-rational closed point, so this excludes the entire nonnormal locus. Hence $\mathcal B$ and $R[z,z^{-1}]$ are normal. Finally an element of $\operatorname{Frac}R$ integral over $R$ is integral over this Laurent extension and therefore belongs to it; its Laurent expansion has only the degree-zero coefficient, so it belongs to $R$. This proves normality of $R$. When $m=0$, $R=k$ directly; all other boundary cases are included in the filtration argument.

derivations.claim: A matrix has rank at most $m$ exactly when all $(m+1)$-minors vanish, by Gaussian elimination. Thus the symmetric zero locus is precisely the asserted set. The factorial is nonzero in characteristic zero. In the canonical form consisting of $r/2$ symplectic blocks, this exterior power is zero exactly when $r\le2n=m$. Combined with step 1.1, their zero sets are exactly the stated rank-bounded loci. Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and let $t\ge1$. For each integer $0\le m\le t$, in the polynomial ring of a generic symmetric $t\times t$ matrix $Z$, the ideal $I_{m+1}$ generated by all $(m+1)$-minors is prime and its zero set is the locus $\operatorname{rank}Z\le m$; $k[Z]/I_{m+1}$ is normal. For each even integer $0\le m\le t$, in the polynomial ring of a generic alternating $t\times t$ matrix $A$, the ideal $J_{m+2}$ generated by the principal Pfaffians of size $m+2$ is prime and its zero set is the locus $\operatorname{rank}A\le m$; $k[A]/J_{m+2}$ is normal. When the indicated generator size exceeds $t$, the corresponding ideal is zero and the quotient is polynomial.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic zero and let $t\ge0$. Let $V$ have dimension $m\ge1$ with a nondegenerate symmetric form $B$, or dimension $m=2n\ge2$ with a nondegenerate alternating form $B$. Symmetric means $B(v,w)=B(w,v)$; alternating means $B(v,v)=0$ for every $v$; nondegenerate means that $B(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in V$ implies $v=0$. Write $GL(V)$ for the group of invertible linear maps on $V$, and set $O(V,B)=\{g\in GL(V):B(gv,gw)=B(v,w)\}$ and, in the alternating case, $Sp(V,B)=\{g\in GL(V):B(gv,gw)=B(v,w)\}$; these denote the full isometry groups. The Gram map sends $(v_1,\ldots,v_t)\in V^t$ to $(B(v_i,v_j))_{i,j}\in\operatorname{Mat}_t(k)$. Its image is the set of symmetric, respectively alternating, matrices of rank at most $\min(m,t)$. When $t\ge m$, every Gram matrix of rank $m$ has a single fiber orbit under the stated group, and the stabilizer of each tuple in that orbit is trivial. For even $r$, let $J_r$ denote the block diagonal matrix with $r/2$ copies of $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$; let $I_r$ denote the $r\times r$ identity matrix. For $0\le r\le\min(m,t)$, the rank-$r$ symmetric stratum has dimension $rt-r(r-1)/2$; for even $0\le r\le\min(m,t)$, the rank-$r$ alternating stratum has dimension $rt-r(r+1)/2$.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then the polynomial ring $R[x]$ is a
Noetherian commutative ring.

No hypothesis beyond Noetherianity is placed on $R$: it may have zero divisors,
and it may be the zero ring.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then

1. $R/I$ is Noetherian for every ideal $I$ of $R$
   ([[def-quotient-ring]]), and
2. $S^{-1}R$ is Noetherian for every multiplicative subset $S\subseteq R$
   ([[def-multiplicative-subset-and-localisation]]).

Both cases include their degenerate instances: $I=R$ makes $R/I$ the zero ring,
and $0\in S$ makes $S^{-1}R$ the zero ring, and the zero ring is Noetherian.

Assume AC. Let $A$ be a Noetherian normal domain ([[def-normal-noetherian-ring]]) with fraction field $K$, so that $A$ is integrally closed in $K$. Then, inside $K$,
$$A=\bigcap_{\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=1}A_{\mathfrak p},$$
the intersection running over all height-one prime ideals $\mathfrak p$ of $A$. Equivalently, a rational function which is regular at every height-one point of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is regular.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the Nullstellensatz route. For every ideal $J\subseteq R=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, $I(V(J))=\sqrt J$. Together with $V(I(X))=X$ for algebraic $X$, these are inverse inclusion-reversing bijections between radical ideals and algebraic sets. Nonempty irreducible algebraic sets correspond precisely to proper prime ideals, and points to maximal ideals. The empty set corresponds to $R$. For $A=R/I(X)$ the same correspondence identifies radical ideals of $A$ with closed subsets of $X$; in particular $I_X(V_X(H))=\sqrt H$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M$ be an $R$-module. The module $M$ is **flat** if the functor $-\otimes_RM$ preserves exact sequences: whenever $A\to B\to C$ is exact, so is

$$A\otimes_RM\longrightarrow B\otimes_RM\longrightarrow C\otimes_RM.$$

Since tensoring is always right exact ([[thm-right-exactness-of-tensor-products]], [[def-exact-and-short-exact-sequences-of-modules]]), the definition asks for the remaining left-hand exactness. Its equivalent formulation as preservation of injections is proved separately rather than built into the definition.

The module $M$ is **faithfully flat** if a sequence of $R$-modules is exact exactly when its tensor with $M$ is exact.

For a unital ring homomorphism $f:R\to S$ ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) between commutative rings, $S$ is an $R$-module by $r\cdot s=f(r)s$. The map $f$ is **flat**, respectively **faithfully flat**, when this $R$-module is flat, respectively faithfully flat.

Let $A$ be a commutative ring. An $A$-algebra $B$ is **standard étale** if
there is a polynomial $P\in A[T]$ with $P$ **monic** and an element $g\in A[T]$
such that
$$B\cong \bigl(A[T]/(P)\bigr)_g$$
as $A$-algebras and the image of the formal derivative $P'$ is a **unit** of
$B$. Equivalently (with $P$ monic and the isomorphism fixed), $P'$ has
invertible image in $\bigl(A[T]/(P)\bigr)_g$ if and only if $g^n\in(P')$ for
some $n\ge0$, where $(P')$ denotes the ideal of $A[T]/(P)$ generated by the
image of $P'$; this is the form in which the condition is usually verified.

Two conventions belong to the definition. First, $P$ is required to be monic,
so $A[T]/(P)$ is a free $A$-module with basis $1,T,\dots,T^{\deg P-1}$ by
division with remainder, before any localisation is performed; the localised
algebra $\bigl(A[T]/(P)\bigr)_g$ itself need not be finite over $A$. Second,
the presentation is part of the data: the same $A$-algebra can be standard
étale through one presentation and not visibly standard étale through another,
and the condition is required to hold for at least one monic presentation with
unit derivative. A standard étale algebra is étale over $A$ in the sense of
[[def-etale-morphism-schemes]] when $A\to B$ is finitely presented, which it is
here because $A[T]/(P)$ is a finitely presented $A$-algebra and localisation
preserves finite presentation; the derivative condition is the Jacobian
condition of the single equation $P$ computed by
[[lem-ag-polynomial-quotient-differentials]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $f:X\to S$ and $g:Y\to X$ be morphisms of
schemes and let $h:S'\to S$ be an arbitrary morphism, with base change
$f_{S'}:X\times_SS'\to S'$ ([[def-base-change-morphism-schemes]]).

1. If $f$ is étale ([[def-etale-morphism-schemes]]), then $f_{S'}$ is étale.
2. If $f$ and $g$ are étale, then the composite $f\circ g:Y\to S$ is étale.
3. Pointwise: if $f$ is étale at $x=g(y)$ and $g$ is étale at $y$, then
   $f\circ g$ is étale at $y$; and if $f$ is étale at $x$ then $f_{S'}$ is
   étale at every point of $X\times_SS'$ lying over $x$.

The relative dimension zero is preserved by base change because the geometric
fibres of the base change are geometric fibres of $f$ after a further field
extension, and it is additive under composition because relative dimensions
add and $0+0=0$. Empty sources and empty fibres cause no exception.

Let $R\to S$ be a faithfully flat homomorphism of commutative rings, and let $N$
be an $R$-module. Then $N$ is flat over $R$ if and only if $N\otimes_R S$ is
flat over $S$.

derivations.claim: We first prove independence under the Gram substitution in every rank $r\ge1$. Put $Z=XX^{\mathsf T}$, where $X=(x_{ic})$ is a generic $t\times r$ matrix, and order variables lexicographically by columns first: $x_{11}>\cdots>x_{t1}>x_{12}>\cdots>x_{tr}$. Cauchy–Binet says $p(A,B)(XX^{\mathsf T})=\sum_{C\subseteq[r],\,|C|=s}\det X_{A,C}\det X_{B,C}$ for $|A|=|B|=s\le r$. For completeness, this identity follows by expanding each entry $z_{ij}=\sum_c x_{ic}x_{jc}$ in the Leibniz determinant: group terms by the chosen column indices; repeated indices cancel by pairing permutations exchanging them, and the terms with one fixed set $C$ give the two displayed determinants. A determinant's leading monomial pairs the smallest available row with its first column, then the next row with its next column, recursively. Comparing column sets in this sum, the largest summand has $C=(1,\ldots,s)$. Thus the minor has leading monomial $\prod_{c=1}^s x_{a_cc}x_{b_cc}$ with coefficient one.

For a standard product, remove empty factors and reverse the sequence of its columns to obtain $B_q,A_q,\ldots,B_1,A_1$. Column lengths are nonincreasing, rows are weakly increasing by the standard-chain inequalities, and columns are strictly increasing. Each column length occurs an even number of times, so all row lengths are even. Conversely a semistandard tableau with even row lengths has an even number of columns of each length: those numbers are consecutive differences of even row lengths. Pairing consecutive equal-height columns and reversing their sequence gives a unique standard product. Finally its Gram leading monomial from step 1.1 records the entries in each tableau row, and weak increase uniquely reconstructs each row from those multiplicities. Distinct standard products with minor sizes at most $r$ therefore have distinct leading monomials and are linearly independent after the rank-$r$ Gram substitution.

Take $r=t$ in step 2.1. A standard product of polynomial degree $d$ corresponds exactly to an even-row tableau with $2d$ boxes and entries in $[t]$. By [F1], the number of these is $\binom{N+d-1}{d}$, where $N=t(t+1)/2$. This equals the dimension of the degree-$d$ homogeneous part of the polynomial ring in the $N$ entries of $Z$: the monomials $z^e$ are indexed by $e\in\mathbb N^N$ with $\sum e_{ij}=d$. Step 2.1 proves independence of all these standard products already in this polynomial ring, because a linear relation there would remain a relation under Gram substitution. An independent set of the full finite dimension is a basis. Consequently the standard products of all minor sizes span the polynomial ring in every degree.

We make the resulting identities completely indexed and constructive. Let $\mathcal E_d=\{e=(e_{ij})_{i\le j}:\sum e_{ij}=d\}$ and let $\mathcal T_d$ be the standard products of degree $d$, without empty factors; order both finite sets lexicographically in any fixed encoding. For a product $Q=\prod_{h=1}^q p(A_h,B_h)$, with $s_h=|A_h|=|B_h|$ and $\sum_hs_h=d$, define $b_e(Q)=\sum_{\sigma_h\in\mathfrak S_{s_h}}\prod_h\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma_h)$, where the sum is restricted by the following explicit indexing condition: the multiset of unordered pairs $\{\min(a_{hc},b_{h,\sigma_h(c)}),\max(a_{hc},b_{h,\sigma_h(c)})\}$, over all $h$ and $1\le c\le s_h$, contains $(i,j)$ exactly $e_{ij}$ times. An empty restricted sum is zero. Leibniz expansion gives exactly $Q=\sum_{e\in\mathcal E_d}b_e(Q)z^e$. Form the square integer matrix $M_d=(b_e(T))_{e\in\mathcal E_d,T\in\mathcal T_d}$. It is invertible over $\mathbb Q$ by step 3.1 applied over an algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q$. Since its nonzero determinant is an integer and $k$ has characteristic zero, it is invertible over $k$ as well.

If $M_d[T\leftarrow b(Q)]$ denotes the matrix with column $T$ replaced by $(b_e(Q))_e$, the explicit straightening identity is $Q=\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_d}\bigl(\det M_d[T\leftarrow b(Q)]/\det M_d\bigr)T$. Indeed multiplying the coefficient vector on the right by $M_d$ gives $b(Q)$ by [F2] applied to the finite square matrix $M_d$ over $k$, so its coefficient of each monomial $z^e$ is precisely the coefficient on the left. All sets, entries, signs, and denominators in this identity have been specified by finite ordered index data; no existence of a straightening law is assumed. Applying it once replaces any nonstandard product directly by standard products, so no further nonstandard term is produced and rewriting terminates. For $d=0$ both indexing sets consist of the unit and the matrix is $(1)$.

Return to $0<m<t$. Every minor of size $s\ge m+1$ lies in $I_{m+1}$. Explicitly, for increasing $A,B$ of size $s$, write $A'=\{a_1,\ldots,a_{m+1}\}$. Laplace expansion along those rows is $p(A,B)=\sum_{C\subseteq B,\,|C|=m+1}(-1)^{(m+1)(m+2)/2+\sum_{b_j\in C}j}\,p(A',C)p(A\setminus A',B\setminus C)$, with the zero-size determinant interpreted as one. Each summand contains a generating $(m+1)$-minor. Thus step 5.1, followed by discarding every standard product containing such a minor, spans the quotient by standard products with all sizes at most $m$. All generators of $I_{m+1}$ vanish under the rank-$m$ Gram substitution, so a relation among these surviving classes would contradict their Gram independence from step 2.1. They form a basis, and the same finite indexed identities, reduced modulo the ideal, supply terminating straightening there. For $m=0$, the quotient by the ideal of entries is $k$ and the only allowed product is the unit. For $m\ge t$, the ideal is zero and steps 3.1–5.1 give the polynomial-ring assertion.

derivations.claim: We first construct the original, sum-skein version over $F=\mathbb Q(b,t)$. Set $h=(b+b^{-1})/t-1$. Its desired normalization is $L(\bigcirc)=1$, positive and negative curls have factors $b,b^{-1}$, an extra trivial circle has factor $h$, and its skein equation is $L(D)+L(S_cD)=tC_c(D)$, where $S_c$ switches crossing $c$ and $C_c(D)=L(E_cD)+L(e_cD)$ is the sum over its two smoothings. All constructions are by induction on the crossing number $N$. At a given $N$, first define single-component diagrams; then define diagrams with increasing numbers of components. The crossing-free value on $r\ge1$ circles is $h^{r-1}$. Throughout the induction the lower-crossing functions satisfy the stated equations and invariance under moves whose diagrams have fewer than $N$ crossings.

Assuming the function known below $N$, switching crossing $c$ transports a proposed value $x$ to $T_c(x)=-x+tC_c(D)$. Repeating this switch is the identity because its two smoothings do not depend on the crossing sign. Two switches $c,j$ commute as transports: applying the lower-crossing skein relation at the remaining crossing in each smoothing gives $C_c(D)+C_c(S_jD)=t\sum_{u\in\{E_c,e_c\},v\in\{E_j,e_j\}}L(uvD)=C_j(D)+C_j(S_cD)$. Consequently $T_jT_c(x)=x-tC_c(D)+tC_j(S_cD)=x-tC_j(D)+tC_c(S_jD)=T_cT_j(x)$. Thus an expansion along a fixed set of switches is independent of their order. Explicitly, for an ordered list $c_1,\ldots,c_k$ and $D_j=S_{c_j}\cdots S_{c_1}D$, its value obtained from a prescribed terminal value $u(D_k)$ is $(-1)^ku(D_k)+t\sum_{j=1}^k(-1)^{j-1}C_{c_j}(D_{j-1})$. This identity follows successively from the two-term transport rule, so it uses only already-defined evaluations of diagrams with at most $N-1$ crossings.

For a directed point $p$ on a one-component diagram, switch exactly those crossings first encountered underneath when following the component from $p$. The terminal diagram $U_p$ is descending and is an unknot: lift its traversed part above the untraversed part and draw that part away successively until only framing curls remain. Give it terminal value $b^{w(U_p)}$, where $w$ is oriented writhe. Define $Q(D,p)$ by the switch expansion of step 2.1 with this terminal value, and define $L(D)=(Q(D,p)+Q(D,\bar p))/2$, where $\bar p$ reverses the direction at the same point. Use this average also when $D$ is descending for one directed point; $b^{w(U_p)}$ is a terminal scalar, not a second prescription for $L(D)$. For a multi-component diagram having a component over all the others, prescribe $L(D)=hL(C)L(D-C)$, with $C$ considered alone. If no component is over all the others, for every component $C$ choose a point and either direction, switch its undercrossings with other components so that it lies over all the others, and use terminal value $hL(C)L(D-C)$. Define $L(D)$ as the average of these $2r$ switch expansions, where $r$ is the number of components. The terminal factors are already defined: single-component diagrams are defined first at level $N$, and deleting one component decreases component number if the remaining crossing number is still $N$. The expansion sums have fewer crossings.

The multi-component switch set for lifting a fixed component is independent of point and direction, so step 2.1 makes its expansion independent of these choices. For a knot, moving the point past one encounter with a crossing toggles exactly that crossing in the descending switch set. The two terminal descending diagrams differ by switching this crossing, which is the first or last encounter from the new point. Their terminal values satisfy the required sum-skein equation: if their writhes are $v+1,v-1$, the two smoothings have values $b^v$ and $hb^v$. To see this, the smoothing that separates the traversed initial portion produces two descending unknots with one over the other; the other is their connected sum with possibly one direction reversed. Their total self-writhe is $v$, since the mutual crossing-sign sum of the two separated portions is zero: one lies over the other, and their algebraic planar intersection number is zero. Both diagrams reduce by pulling these overlying arcs away, followed by removing curls, so their evaluations follow from lower-crossing invariance and curl factors. The equation is $b^{v+1}+b^{v-1}=t(1+h)b^v$. By commuting the toggled switch to the beginning of the expansion, this terminal equality makes $Q(D,p)$ unchanged. Moving the point around all arcs proves point independence. Averaging the two directions makes direction independence explicit. Agreement with the terminal scalar on descending diagrams is deferred until after regular-isotopy invariance; point independence alone does not identify the two directed expansions.

The resulting function satisfies the sum-skein equation at every crossing. For a knot choose the directed point so the selected crossing is first in the expansion of the diagram in which it is incorrect; the two expansions differ by that initial transport, giving the equation. For a link, compare the expansions used in step 3.1. If the crossing is a self-crossing of the component being lifted, apply the lower-complexity equation to its single-component terminal factor and to every smoothing term. If it belongs only to the remaining link, apply the equation to that terminal factor and to every smoothing term. If its two strands lie on different components and the lifted component is one of them, commute that crossing to the first switch position; the two terminal lift diagrams agree and the initial transport gives the equation. If the lifted component is neither one, the lower-crossing equation applies to all smoothing terms and to the remaining-link factor. For clarity, the consistency with an already overlying component has a separate two-layer comparison. Suppose $A$ is above the rest and the selected lift is $B$. Commute the switches of $B$ with components other than $A$ before its mutual switches with $A$. Smoothing one of these earlier switches leaves $A$ over the resulting lower-crossing diagram, so induction factors out $hL(A)$; their alternating sum is exactly the lift expansion for $D-A$. For the remaining comparison both $A$ and $B$ are above the remaining link $R$. If $R$ is nonempty, every smoothing of an $A,B$ crossing merges them into a single component above $R$; induction factors its value as $hL(R)$ times its isolated knot value. Both terminal orders have the identical value $h^2L(A)L(B)L(R)$. If $R$ is empty, there is no factor $hL(R)$ to extract, and both terminal orders instead have value $hL(A)L(B)$. It remains to compare the two-component lift expansion with $hL(A)L(B)$. Switch self-crossings in $A$ and $B$ until each is descending; the difference of these two quantities changes sign under each such switch, since every smoothing correction has fewer crossings and agrees by induction. For descending $A,B$ with $A$ above $B$, straighten the descending two-component diagram to two disjoint circles by nonincreasing moves and curl removals. This comparison respects each such move directly at the level of its switch expansion: for a cancelling crossing pair $u,v$, the correction is $t(C_u(D)-C_v(S_uD))=0$, since the two opening smoothings agree and the other two give the same signed curl; a move III changes the order of two switches and is exactly the transport-square identity of step 2.1, with its smoothed diagrams related by a cancelling pair. Terminal writhe and scalar products obey the same curl factors. Thus the difference is zero at the end and hence at the start. This proves the required two-component comparison, and then the preceding factorizations prove the direct-overlying prescription for the original link. Every averaging summand therefore obeys the same skein equation.

To verify the curl rule, place the point outside the curl and commute its switch, if any, to the end of the expansion. At lower crossing number the skein equation and descending values recover every directed expansion from $L$, by step 2.1 and induction. For either direction, if the curl of sign $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ is first encountered over, its terminal factor is $b^\varepsilon$ and every smoothing outside the curl retains it, giving $b^\varepsilon L(D_0)$, where $D_0$ has the curl removed. If first encountered under, switch it; the switched curl has factor $b^{-\varepsilon}$ by the preceding case. Its two smoothings are $D_0$ and $D_0\sqcup\bigcirc$, so the transport gives $(-b^{-\varepsilon}+t(1+h))L(D_0)=b^\varepsilon L(D_0)$. Here the lower-crossing circle rule applies, and $t(1+h)=b+b^{-1}$. This proves the curl rule for both directed summands and hence their average; the component-lift products give the same calculation for links. An extra disjoint circle contributes $h$ in every terminal product and every smoothing term, so induction gives the circle rule as well. A descending arc can be pulled away without adding crossings by moves III and cancelling pairs by moves II, leaving curls. When used in step 4.1 these reductions concern diagrams with fewer than $N$ crossings, so they use only the induction hypothesis.

For move II, switching both crossings of a cancellable bigon leaves the evaluation unchanged. Indeed, expand at one crossing and then the other: the switched-diagram terms have positive combined sign, and the two smoothing sums cancel. The smoothings in which the bigon opens are the same diagram on either expansion; the other two smoothings each produce the same curl of the same sign on the same strand, so their values agree by step 6.1. Choose the basepoint and component lift so that the overpassing local arc is traversed or lifted first. Neither crossing is then switched in that local portion; all switches occur outside it, each smoothing term has fewer crossings, and the terminal descending or layered product loses the bigon without changing its writhe or factors. Induction gives invariance. If the chosen lift instead meets the underpassing arc, use the just-proved simultaneous switching identity to make it the overpassing arc; the same argument applies. This covers a bigon on one component and on two distinct components, and proves both directions of move II.

For move III, label the three local arcs by their height order. First give them the height order in which they are first encountered in a chosen traversal or component-lift expansion. There are then no local switches, and corresponding switches outside the disk produce identical terminal values and lower-crossing smoothing terms related by the same move, giving invariance by induction. The six possible height orders are connected by exchanging adjacent heights. Such an exchange switches one corresponding crossing on both sides of the move. Apply the sum-skein equation at those crossings: each sum of the old and switched evaluations is $t$ times a pair of smoothing evaluations. The two pairs agree. One smoothing cancels the two remaining crossings by move II or identifies them by planar isotopy; the other slides a cup past them. Here is an endpoint description of the cup slide, independent of any BMW presentation. In the following diagram words the factors are stacked from top to bottom in their written left-to-right order. In a three-strand rectangle let $e_j$ denote the actual crossing-free cup and cap joining adjacent positions $j,j+1$, and $x_j$ the actual crossing at those positions. The diagrams $e_1x_2x_1$ and $x_2x_1e_2$ both reduce to the diagram with upper cup $(1,2)$, lower cap $(2',3')$, and an untwisted strand from $3$ to $1'$. Slide the arc attached to the cup across the two crossing disks; the two successive over/under encounters then bound a bigon and cancel by move II. Likewise $x_1x_2e_1$ and $e_2x_1x_2$ reduce to upper cup $(2,3)$, lower cap $(1',2')$, and the strand from $1$ to $3'$. Reflecting the crossing data gives the same cancellations for $x_1^{-1},x_2^{-1}$. These are identities of the smoothed diagrams by planar deformation and move II, concerning at most $N-1$ crossings, rather than assumed identities in an abstract algebra. Thus the equality of old evaluations is equivalent to equality of switched evaluations. The adjacent-height exchanges reach every type III configuration, proving move III invariance for every traversal, component choice and outside diagram. Consequently a descending knot $U$ now has $L(U)=b^{w(U)}$: pull its descending arc away by nonincreasing moves II and III until only curls remain, then use step 6.1. This uses the just-proved invariance at $N$, not a direct prescription in step 3.1. Finally expand the established skein equation along the switches for any directed point $p$. The terminal value is now $L(U_p)=b^{w(U_p)}$, so step 2.1 gives $Q(D,p)=L(D)$, for both directions. Thus the average agrees with every directed expansion, including on descending knots. This closes the simultaneous crossing-number induction over $F$.

Extend the field by $i^2=-1$, replace $b$ by $ia$ and $t$ by $-is$, and for a nonempty unoriented diagram $D$ temporarily choose orientations and put $D^\flat(D)=-i^{-w(D)}(-1)^{c(D)}L(D;ia,-is)$, where $c(D)$ is its number of components. This does not depend on orientations. Reversing one whole component changes writhe by minus twice its mutual crossing-sign sum with all the other components, hence by a multiple of four by [F2]. The phase is unchanged. The same formula is unchanged by moves II and III because writhe and component number are unchanged by these moves and $L$ is invariant. A positive curl multiplies the phase by $i^{-1}$ and $L$ by $ia$, giving factor $a$; a negative curl gives $i(ia)^{-1}=a^{-1}$. Its value on one trivial circle is $1$.

We verify the difference-skein signs rather than importing the Dubrovnik conversion. If the chosen global orientations make the crossing in $L_+$ negative, interchange $L_+,L_-$ and also $L_0,L_\infty$; proving the equation after both interchanges is equivalent to the original equation. We may therefore take this crossing positive and write $w=w(L_+)$ and $c=c(L_+)$. Switching gives writhe $w-2$ and the same component number, so $D^\flat(L_+)-D^\flat(L_-)=-i^{-w}(-1)^c(L(L_+)+L(L_-))$. The sum-skein equation gives the common factor $(-i^{-w}(-1)^c)(-is)$ times the sum of the two smoothing evaluations. For the oriented smoothing $L_0$, writhe is $w-1$ and component parity reverses; its phase is therefore exactly $(-i^{-w}(-1)^c)(-i)$. The other smoothing has the opposite phase. If the original crossing is between distinct components, orient it after first reversing one entire incident component: that changes writhe by a multiple of four, changes the removed crossing to negative, and merging gives writhe congruent to $w+1$ modulo four and reverses component parity. If the crossing is a self-crossing, the oriented smoothing splits its component into two; to orient the other smoothing reverse one of these portions. Their mutual crossing-sign sum is even by [F2], so this reversal changes the remaining writhe by a multiple of four. The other smoothing then has writhe congruent to $w-1$ and retains component parity. In both cases its phase is the negative of the phase for $L_0$. A polynomial ring $B[x]$ over a UFD $B$ is a UFD: factor the content using factorization in $B$, factor its primitive part over $\operatorname{Frac}(B)[x]$ by [F5], and clear denominators and contents of the factors. Their product is primitive by [F4], so comparison of contents makes the remaining scalar a unit of $B$. Starting from $\mathbb Z$ by [F3] and iterating proves $\mathbb Z[a,d,s]$ is a UFD. Inverting $a$ and $d$ preserves this property: factor each numerator, discard factors associated to $a$ or $d$ since they become units, and compare two such factorizations by clearing powers of $a,d$ and using uniqueness in the polynomial ring. A remaining prime stays prime because divisibility after clearing those powers is ordinary divisibility by a prime different from $a,d$. Thus $B=\mathbb Z[a^{\pm1},d^{\pm1}]$ and $B[s]$ are UFDs. The element $d-1$ is prime in $B$, since substituting $d=1$ has kernel $(d-1)$ and domain quotient $\mathbb Z[a^{\pm1}]$. It does not divide $a-a^{-1}$, whose value at $d=1$ is nonzero. Hence $f=s(d-1)-(a-a^{-1})$ is primitive over $B$, and it is irreducible over $\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ because it is linear. By [F4] it is irreducible and therefore prime in $B[s]$. Its quotient $A$ is a domain. Its localization at the nonzero element $s$ is injective: $s^ku=0$ in a domain implies $u=0$. Eliminating $d$ there gives a subring of $\mathbb Q(i)(a,s)$ with $d=1+(a-a^{-1})/s$, and thus the claimed injection. No choice principle is needed in these finite factorizations.

In fact every value $P(D)$ belongs to $A$. Induct on crossing number, and at fixed crossing number on the incorrect crossings of a chosen traversal: the difference-skein rule changes an incorrect crossing to a correct one plus two diagrams with fewer crossings, with coefficients $\pm s$. A fully descending diagram is a disjoint union of unknots with framing curls, so its value is a product of powers of $a^{\pm1}$ and $d$. The induction therefore uses only coefficients in $A$. The same reduction proves uniqueness of a function satisfying the stated rules. Extend $P$ linearly to the free $A$-module on diagrams. Its kernel contains the defining skein, curl and loop relations and regular-isotopy differences, so it descends to their quotient; its value on the empty diagram is $1$. The descending reduction shows the empty diagram spans this quotient, and the descended function is a left inverse to the scalar map $A\to KT_0(A)$. This map is consequently injective as well as surjective, proving the freeness assertion.
